text: The Young British Artists, or YBAs—also known as Brit artists or Britart—are a loose collective of visual artists who first exhibited together in London in 1988. Many of the group graduated from the BA Fine Art course at Goldsmiths between 1987 and 1990, with some having trained at the Royal College of Art. The scene originated through artist-led exhibitions held in warehouses and factories, starting with Damien Hirst’s Freeze in 1988, followed by the East Country Yard Show and Modern Medicine in 1990. These exhibitions were notable for their "shock tactics," use of everyday or throwaway materials, wild lifestyles, and an attitude that was both oppositional and entrepreneurial. The group gained significant media attention and dominated British art during the 1990s, with international exhibitions such as Brilliant! and Sensation showcasing their work. Charles Saatchi was a key supporter and collector of many YBAs, though Angus Fairhurst was a notable exception. Leading figures include Damien Hirst and Tracey Emin, with key works such as Hirst’s The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living—a shark preserved in formaldehyde—and Emin’s My Bed, a dishevelled bed surrounded by personal detritus. There is debate over the first use of the term "young British artists": Tate claims it was Michael Corris in a 1992 Artforum footnote, while others argue Saatchi used it in his 1992 exhibition Young British Artists I; the acronym "YBA" was coined in 1994. Most YBAs were born in the mid-1960s. Core group members graduated from Goldsmiths in specific classes: Liam Gillick, Fiona Rae, Steve Park, and Sarah Lucas in 1987; Ian Davenport, Michael Landy, Gary Hume, Anya Gallaccio, Lala Meredith-Vula, Henry Bond, and Angela Bulloch in 1988; Damien Hirst, Angus Fairhurst, Mat Collishaw, Simon Patterson, and Abigail Lane in 1989; Gillian Wearing and Sam Taylor-Wood in 1990; and Jason Martin in 1993. Teaching staff during this period included Jon Thompson, Richard Wentworth, Michael Craig-Martin, Ian Jeffrey, Helen Chadwick, Mark Wallinger, Judith Cowan, and Glen Baxter. Gavin Turk and Mark Francis, who studied at Chelsea School of Art (1986–1989) and the Royal College of Art (1989–1991), were also part of the group and exhibited in the Saatchi Sensation show. Freeze, organized by Hirst during his second year of study, was held in a London Docklands warehouse and lacked major press coverage but inspired the model of artist-as-curator, influencing later independent spaces. A smaller precursor, Progress by Degree, organized by Angus Fairhurst, took place shortly before Freeze. In 1990, Henry Bond and Sarah Lucas staged the East Country Yard Show in a 16,000m² warehouse in London Docklands. Art critic Andrew Graham-Dixon noted the shows' ambition and impact, comparing them favorably to exhibitions by the Liverpool Tate. Established alternative spaces like City Racing and Milch, as well as activity in Hoxton/Shoreditch, provided early exposure. The Serpentine Gallery held a survey of the group in 1991 titled Broken English, and in 1992, Charles Saatchi launched a series of exhibitions featuring Sarah Lucas, Rachel Whiteread, and Damien Hirst. A second wave of YBAs emerged in 1992–1993 through exhibitions such as New Contemporaries, New British Summertime, and Minky Manky, including Douglas Gordon, Christine Borland, Fiona Banner, Tracey Emin, Tacita Dean, Georgina Starr, and Jane and Louise Wilson. The 1995 British Art Show included several YBA artists. The YBAs helped revitalize the contemporary art market, spawning commercial galleries such as Karsten Schubert, Sadie Coles, Victoria Miro, Maureen Paley’s Interim Art, and Jay Jopling’s White Cube. Frieze launched in 1991 and embraced the YBAs, while publications like Art Monthly, Art Review, Modern Painters, and Contemporary Art shifted focus to emerging British artists. Charles Saatchi, a major art collector and co-founder of Saatchi and Saatchi, visited Freeze and was astonished by Hirst’s installation A Thousand Years, which he later bought. Saatchi became the primary collector and sponsor of the YBAs, shifting his focus from American and German art to emerging British artists. His collection was exhibited in a converted paint factory in St John’s Wood, inspiring large-scale concept artworks. His 1992 exhibition featured Hirst’s shark, which became a defining work of British art and a global symbol of Britart. The artists gained intense media coverage due to their prominence in the Turner Prize, which had several nominees and winners from the group, amplified by Channel 4’s sponsorship. The group’s status solidified in 1995 with the exhibition Brilliant! at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis. The term "yBa" was used as early as 1994 and later featured in Simon Ford’s 1996 article in Art Monthly. Jay Jopling represented several YBAs, including Jake & Dinos Chapman, Tracey Emin, Marcus Harvey, Damien Hirst, Gary Hume, Marc Quinn, Gavin Turk, and Sam Taylor-Wood, whom he married in 1998. Karsten Schubert was the first major dealer of YBA artists, exhibiting Ian Davenport, Gary Hume, and Michael Landy in November 1988. In 1997, the Royal Academy held Sensation, a show of Saatchi’s private collection that included major YBA works, sparking controversy—especially over Marcus Harvey’s Myra and Chris Ofili’s The Holy Virgin Mary—and leading to three Academicians resigning. In 1997, Gillian Wearing won the Turner Prize; in 1998, Chris Ofili did the same. In 1999, Tracey Emin was nominated, with her exhibit My Bed generating significant media attention and contributing to the rise of the anti-YBA group The Stuckists, co-founded by her ex-boyfriend Billy Childish. In 2003, Jake and Dinos Chapman and Anya Gallaccio were nominated. On 24 May 2004, a fire in a storage warehouse destroyed works from the Saatchi collection, including the Chapman Brothers’ Hell and Tracey Emin’s tent, Everyone I Have Ever Slept With 1963–1995. In 2008, Angus Fairhurst died by suicide. In the 2011 Birthday Honours List, Sam Taylor-Wood and Gillian Wearing were appointed to the Order of the British Empire by Queen Elizabeth II. Several YBAs have been elected as lifetime members of the Royal Academy of Arts, earning the title "Royal Academician" and the designation "RA." Critics such as Richard Cork, Louisa Buck, Sarah Kent, and Sir Nicholas Serota have supported the artists, with Serota advancing their inclusion in the Tate collection. Maureen Paley stated that the YBA generation was defined by boldness and a belief that "you can get away with anything." Iwona Blazwick, director of the Whitechapel Art Gallery, said in 2009 that the YBA moment was over, but that their influence continued to grow. In 1998, John Windsor noted that YBA work seemed tame compared to the "shock art" of the 1970s, such as Mandy Havers’ Pink Crucifixion. In 1999, The Stuckists were founded with an anti-YBA stance. In 2002, Sir Simon Rattle criticized Britart, leading to accusations of poor understanding of conceptual art. Playwright Tom Stoppard and critics like Brian Sewell, David Lee, and Rolf Harris—whom criticized Tracey Emin’s My Bed as a "con"—were hostile to the movement. James Heartfield argued that the 1990s art boom encouraged sloppiness, with YBAs favoring gestures over patient work and using public outrage, which faded quickly. The group is parodied in a Private Eye cartoon strip and in Jilly Cooper’s Pandora. Female artists were a minority in the male-dominated YBA scene; Sarah Lucas, Jenny Saville, and Rachel Whiteread faced underrepresentation and less media attention compared to male peers like Hirst. Feminist influences in the 1980s shaped female YBA work, with artists subverting feminine stereotypes. Rachel Whiteread’s work, such as Nine Tables, exists in a gender-neutral space while still being viewed as feminine, and Daniel Ogilivie linked this to Judith Butler’s theory that the act of casting creates gender. Jenny Saville, influenced by feminist ideology, discovered the absence of women in art history and began painting female nudes that rejected idealization, showing natural flaws like pubic hair and discolored skin. She stated she aimed not to teach but to prompt discussion about how women have been constructed by patriarchal structures, asserting that beauty is often defined by the male image of the female body.

The document examines how women have been shaped by male perspectives. It questions the concept of beauty, stating that beauty is typically defined by the male ideal of the female body. However, it also asserts that the speaker's view of women is that they are beautiful in their individuality.
